headline: Saudi Solar Farm Becomes Unlikely Haven for Endangered Gazelles
meta_description: A 250-megawatt solar installation powering a luxury resort is now sheltering Arabian sand gazelles, with plans to grow the population from 38 to over 500.
summary_short: Saudi conservationists have transformed a massive solar farm into a breeding sanctuary for threatened Arabian sand gazelles, combining renewable energy with wildlife res…
body:
A 250-megawatt solar installation in Saudi Arabia is doing double duty: powering a renewable energy resort while sheltering one of the world's most vulnerable gazelle species. The solar park, spanning 1,200 acres near the Red Sea coast within a 24,500-square-mile nature reserve, now hosts 38 Arabian sand gazelles—animals so rare that only about 3,000 remain in the wild across the Arabian Peninsula and Turkiye. The wildlife-proof fencing surrounding the solar panels creates a protected breeding ground where the gazelles can feed, graze, and reproduce safely from predators, with the panels themselves providing crucial shade that keeps temperatures 8 to 18 degrees cooler than the surrounding desert.

Andrew Zaloumis, director of the reserve, calls this approach "ReWildingVoltaics"—a framework designed to build self-sustaining wildlife populations capable of surviving independently in the wild. The initiative began last October when mountain gazelles and Arabian hares were also released into the solar park. By May, once staff confirmed the animals were thriving, males were introduced to encourage natural breeding. The ambitious goal is to grow the current population of 38 to over 500 gazelles, which would then be reestablished throughout the larger reserve.

This innovation reflects a growing recognition that renewable energy infrastructure needn't simply coexist with nature—it can actively support it. The solar plant serves Amaala, a 100% renewable-powered tourist resort, while simultaneously addressing Saudi Arabia's broader conservation targets: protecting 30 percent of the kingdom's land and sea, and generating half its electricity from renewable sources by 2030. What makes this project remarkable isn't just the ambition, but the practical proof that solar farms can become genuine sanctuaries for species facing extinction.
quick_facts: 38 Arabian sand gazelles now live in the Saudi solar park
Only ~3,000 remain wild across Arabian Peninsula and Turkiye
Solar panels provide 8–18°C cooler shade than open desert
Goal: grow population to 500+ for desert reintroduction
